title: A Language Is Born: Cultural Evolution in the Lab
text: Friday’s seminar, second hour · Today we meet a community of people inventing a language from nothing: making up words for shapes that have never had names, and we ask a simple question: does the size of a community shape the language it builds? Everything runs in RStudio on UCloud; use your Methods01 setup to get started.

title: A Language Is Born: Cultural Evolution in the Lab
text:
The question
Every human language was invented by a community. The words of English are shaped over many generations by people using them with one another. In the lecture, we explored processes of cultural evolution: structure that emerges from use. And these processes raise a question we can actually test. If communities build languages, do the properties of the community leave their fingerprint on the language itself?
Raviv, Meyer and Lev-Ari (2019) brought that question into the laboratory. They gathered communities of volunteers and handed each one a private world to name: a set of novel shapes with no existing words. On every turn, one member saw a shape and typed a made-up word for it; the others chose, from an array, the shape they thought the word meant. Everyone saw whether the guess landed, then they swapped roles, and played again for fourteen rounds in all. Round by round, the invented words drifted from a scramble of private guesses toward a vocabulary the whole community came to share.

  shape they think it means

  
  Both see whether the choice was right, then they swap roles. You always play in pairs, but across the game
  you take turns with every other member of your community, more of them in a larger community.

  
  

  
  Two different conditions: community size

  A community of eight


The design had two main conditions. Some communities had four members; others had eight. That is the only knob the experimenters touched, and the question for today is whether it changed the properties of the languages that grew.
Place a bet before you go on. A community of four is intimate: few people, little to track, easy to fall into step. A community of eight is busier: more partners, more words in play, more to coordinate.
Which community do you think ends up communicating more accurately by the final round: the group of four or eight? Write your guess down and explain why you have chosen it. You will settle this question with the data, in Exercise 1.

title: Exercise 2 · Why the big communities win
section: Task 1: What happens to the length of the words?
text:
Task 1: What happens to the length of the words?
Last week, in the tangram game, descriptions got shorter over time: a whole sentence shrank to “mouse” or “praying monk”. You might expect the same here: as a community settles on its words, the words get snappier.
Let’s check. nchar() gives the number of characters in a piece of text, so nchar(word) is a word’s length. Average it per round:
# For each round, how long is the average word?
word_length <- lang %>%
  filter(word != "") %>%
  group_by(round) %>%                       # the game's clock
  summarise(mean_length = mean(nchar(word)))

word_length
# A tibble: 14 × 2
   round mean_length
   <int>       <dbl>
 1     1         4.5
 2     2         4.8
 3     3         5.3
 4     4         5.7
 5     5         6.2
 6     6         6.4
 7     7         6.5
 8     8         6.5
 9     9         6.7
10    10         6.8
# ℹ 4 more rows

Last week the utterances got shorter. This week, as you can already see in the first ten rounds, shorter again, or longer?

Longer. Words grow from about 4-5 characters in round 1 to around 7 by the end: the opposite of last week. Something different is going on here, and the next two tasks uncover what.

title: Exercise 2 · Why the big communities win
section: Task 2: And bigger communities’ words grow longest
text:
Task 2: And bigger communities’ words grow longest
Split it by community, exactly as you did for accuracy:
lang %>%
  filter(word != "") %>%
  group_by(round, ___) %>%                 # round AND ??
  summarise(mean_length = mean(nchar(word)), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = round, y = mean_length, colour = community)) +   # colour by community
  geom_point() + geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Words grow longer; fastest in the big communities",
       x = "round", y = "mean word length", colour = "community") +
  theme_bw()
The big communities build the longest words: their average climbs past seven characters by the end, while the small communities level off near six. So the big communities communicate better (Exercise 1) and use longer words. Longer could mean harder: more letters to remember, more to get wrong. How can longer words make a community better understood?

title: Exercise 2 · Why the big communities win
section: Task 3: Read the words, and see the structure
text:
Task 3: Read the words, and see the structure
Numbers brought us this far; now let’s read the raw words. Here is group 12 (a big community) and every word it used for one shape family in the final round. We glue them into a single line so the whole set is visible at once:
# Group 12's words for shape family 2, in the final round.
lang %>%
  filter(group == "g12", shape == "2", round == 14, word != "") %>%
  summarise(words = paste(unique(word), collapse = ", ")) %>%
  pull(words)
[1] "fem-hm, fem-gm, fem-mk, fem-ss, fem-aa, fem-hi, fem-ko, fem-to, fem-nn, fem-kk, fem-uu, fem-oo, fem-kn, fem-ai, fem-fe, fem-ot, fem-fw"
Every single one begins the same way: fem-. Back in round 1 this same shape family was a scramble of unrelated guesses: gim, puieg, weeps, huuu, mep (run the chunk again with round == 1 to see the mess it grew out of). By the final round the community has invented a root, fem-, that means “this family of shapes”, and a short suffix on the end to pick out which particular one.
And it goes further. In the same community, a different shape family settled on het- and hoe-, and another on gekki-. One part for the category, one part for the specific item: a word built from meaningful pieces, exactly like foot + ball + er.
That is compositional structure, and it could be an answer to why bigger communities end up communicating better:

The words get longer because they are now built from parts, where once they were single random blobs.
The big communities built the most structure, because a word like fem-mk can be understood by someone you have never met; they only need to know the parts. A private blob like “mouse” works solely with people who were there when you coined it, and in a big community you are always meeting new partners, so the part-based words are the ones that survive.
A language made of reusable parts is easier to learn and use, which is why the big communities ended up communicating better.


The take-home. A bigger community builds a more structured language (words made of reusable parts, where a small community can lean on one-off labels), because its words must work for a constant stream of new partners. Structure is what makes a language learnable by anyone.

title: 2 · Watch a word being born
text:
Look before you count
The same habit as every week: read the raw data before you measure it. Let’s follow a single shape (item 9) through all fourteen rounds, and watch what a community does with it.
There is a snag, though. One shape in one community is 76 separate words, far too many to read as a list. So we collapse them: one line per round, showing the distinct words the community used that round. paste() glues a set of words into a single string, and unique() keeps only the different ones:
# A big community (eight people) naming shape 9, round by round.
lang %>%
  filter(group == "g12", item == "9", word != "") %>%
  group_by(round) %>%
  summarise(words_this_round = paste(unique(word), collapse = ", "))

 4     4 fem-utf, kohuu, fem-oppi, fem, oktt, hut-tt, fem-ki, fem-ii

 6     6 koh-uu, fem-u, fem-uu, fem

 8     8 fem-kk, fem-ki, fem-nn

Read it from the top. Round 1 is a scramble: eight people look at the same shape and type a dozen different things (huuu, mep, fem, fom, peos). There is no word for this shape yet, only guesses. By the middle rounds the guesses start to pull together; everything is now some version of fem-, and by the end the community has all but settled on fem-uu. Through nothing more than using the words and seeing which ones worked, the community grew itself a word.

Now a smaller community
The same shape (item 9) but this time in a community of four:
# A small community (four people) naming the same shape.
lang %>%

  group_by(round) %>%
  summarise(words_this_round = paste(unique(word), collapse = ", "))
# A tibble: 14 × 2
   round words_this_round
   <int> <chr>
 1     1 poik, piok, poki, ikie, pokie
 2     2 sopoe, ikkie, popo, poik
 3     3 waes, poik, hotaap
 4     4 poiki, kokii
 5     5 poik, pokuuu
 6     6 poik, poikuuu
 7     7 poikuu, poik

10    10 poik
11    11 poiku, poik
12    12 waesu, poik
13    13 poik

This community settled too (on poik). The same shape, named from scratch by two sets of strangers, became two completely different words: fem-uu here, poik there. A word that works perfectly inside one community would mean nothing in the other. Each one grew its own.






🤔 Think first



No one in a community could see the others’ screens or agree on a word out loud. So how does a shared word take hold at all: what is the single piece of information each person gets about whether their word was a good one?






Check your thinking





The only signal is whether the partner picked the right shape. A word that gets understood gets used again; a word that fails gets dropped or tweaked. Across many rounds, the words that survive are the ones that worked: the community comes to agree by keeping what succeeds and letting the rest fall away. Selection, round after round. That is the engine of this whole experiment, and of cultural evolution itself.





Your turn. Pick any other shape (item from 1 to 28) and any community (a big one ("g01" to "g12") or a small one ("g13" to "g24")), and run the same code. Does it settle on a word too? Try one big and one small, and keep a question in mind for what comes next: does one of them seem to agree faster than the other?

title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text: Friday’s seminar, second hour · You just played the game. Now we analyse data from people who played it before you: first 83 pairs, then 104 groups of two to six people, where one person describes for up to five matchers at once. Everything runs in RStudio on UCloud. Use your Methods01 procedure for setting up the code.

title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text:
The question
An hour ago, describing a tangram likely took you a whole sentence. By round six, a couple of words did the same job, and your partner found the right picture faster. Somewhere in those rounds, the two of you built something: names for the shapes that only you two share, resting on everything you now both know about what worked before. That growing pool of shared knowledge is what yesterday’s lecture called common ground, and the private names are conventions: agreements about what words mean.
Grice’s idea from yesterday connects the two: speakers say as much as is needed, and no more. In round one, a lot is needed. Your partner knows nothing yet. By round six, almost nothing is needed, because the common ground carries most of the load. Fewer words, more understanding. What is needed, then, tends to shrink as common ground grows.
That’s the story for two people. But what happens if you need to build common ground with a whole group at once? Describing for five listeners is a different job: they don’t all know the same things, they can’t all ask questions, and a name that clicks for one of them may mean nothing to the rest.
So today has two questions.

When two people talk about the same things again and again, what happens to the words they use?
What changes when the audience grows?

We’ll use data from two published studies of exactly this game. In the first, 83 pairs played it over online chat, so every message they typed is preserved (Hawkins, Frank & Goodman, 2020). In the second, the same game was played by 104 groups of two to six people — one describer, the rest matching (Boyce, Hawkins, Goodman & Frank, 2024).

title: Building Common Ground: The Tangram Task
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this seminar, you will be able to:

Trace how referring expressions compress across repeated reference, in raw messages and in numbers.
Show that pairs say less while understanding more, and explain why that isn’t a paradox.
Compare experimental conditions: what does audience size do to compression and to understanding?
Match a measure to the right unit, and say why words-per-message and words-per-description can tell different stories.

section: Task 1: The measure has to match the unit
text:
Task 1: The measure has to match the unit
In this dataset, the describer often sends several short messages for one shape rather than one long one, so we want the total words spent on each shape each round. That means two steps: sum the words within each trial, then average those totals per group size and round.
# Step 1: total describer words in each trial.
per_trial <- multiparty %>%
  group_by(group, group_size, repetition, trial) %>%
  summarise(words = sum(n_words), .groups = "drop")

# Step 2: average those totals, per group size and round.
red_multi <- per_trial %>%
  group_by(group_size, repetition) %>%
  summarise(mean_words = mean(words), .groups = "drop")

red_multi

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
section: Task 2: Five curves on one plot
text:
Task 2: Five curves on one plot
Putting colour = inside aes() draws a separate line for each value of a variable. Here, one line per group size. We wrap it in factor() so R treats the sizes as five distinct categories to colour, not as numbers on a scale:
ggplot(red_multi, aes(x = repetition, y = mean_words,
                      colour = factor(group_size))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Everyone gets shorter, but big groups take a little longer",
       x = "repetition", y = "mean words per description",
       colour = "group size") +
  theme_bw()

Every line falls to about the same place by round six. Do all the groups get there at the same speed, or do some shrink faster than others?

The bigger the group, the slower the shrink. Everyone lands near the floor by round six. Pairs around 5 words, six-player groups around 7, but they get there very differently: at round three, pairs are already down to about 11 words while six-player groups are still near 18. Common ground with five people is slower to form than with one.

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
section: Task 3: What does the crowd cost in accuracy?
text:
Task 3: What does the crowd cost in accuracy?
Now the other half: did the bigger groups understand as well? One care-step first. n_correct is recorded on every message in a trial, so the same trial’s score appears several times. We want each trial counted once. distinct() keeps one row per trial:
multiparty %>%
  distinct(group, trial, .keep_all = TRUE) %>%   # one row per trial, not per message
  group_by(group_size, repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_correct = 100 * mean(n_correct / n_matchers)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = repetition, y = pct_correct,
             colour = factor(group_size))) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(title = "Pairs reach near-perfect. Big groups never quite do",
       x = "repetition", y = "% of matchers correct",
       colour = "group size") +
  theme_bw()
% matchers correct, size x repetition:
repetition      2     3     4     5     6
1            82    83    84    78    80
2            89    87    88    84    85
6            97    91    87    83    86
Pairs finish near 97% correct. Six-player groups level off in the mid-80s, and they got there using slightly more words. More said, less understood, per listener: the mirror image of what pairs achieved.

title: 2 · The replication: two’s company
text:
Discuss with your neighbour
Why would five matchers make common ground harder to build?

Where this leaves the theory. The core finding held at every group size: describe something repeatedly and the description shrinks. That’s a robust phenomenon. But how fast it shrinks depends on the audience. Common ground is built through back-and-forth, and that back-and-forth gets thinner when it’s split five ways.

Done, or still curious? Open questions.

Two columns are easy to confuse, so it’s worth pausing on them. trial counts every turn in the game, 1 to 72, with all twelve shapes jumbled together. repetition is different: it counts how many times this pair has dealt with one particular shape. Before counting anything, look at the raw data: the same habit as last week. Here is one pair’s director describing one shape, tangram B, every one of the six times it came up:

  filter(pair == "pair01", role == "director", tangram == "") %>%
  select(repetition, message)

1          1 this one kinda looks like they are looking a little down and kneeling with both arms out

That shared, growing store of “things we both know now” is the common ground from yesterday’s lecture, and you can watch them building it in real time. title: 4 · Finding an island
text: Block 3 · From how long the utterance is to what’s inside. We will have a look at how Anne’s WANT island develops through twelve months of speech.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
section: From how long to what’s inside
text:
From how long to what’s inside
MLU told you Anne’s utterances got longer but nothing about the content of her utterances. Time to look inside, and the reading tells you what to look for. On Tomasello’s account, a two-year-old doesn’t have “verbs” as a category: each verb is its own little island: a fixed part plus a slot, learned as a unit from use. Want + thing. More + thing.If that’s right, Anne’s speech should contain a pattern: the same frame, over and over, with different things dropped into the slot.
That’s a checkable claim, and checking it means collecting every “want” Anne ever produced and laying them side by side. For that, we need a new function.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
str_detect()
str_detect(text, pattern) returns TRUE if the text contains the pattern. Wrap the pattern in \\b (word boundary) to match whole words only, and use (a|b) to match either of two words:
str_detect("want some juice", "\\bwant\\b")     # TRUE
str_detect("she wanted it",   "\\bwant\\b")     # FALSE - "wanted" is a different word
str_detect("wanna go",        "\\b(want|wanna)\\b")  # TRUE - matches either

What does str_detect("look at the snow", "no") return, without the \\b?

TRUE: s-no-w. Without boundaries the pattern matches anywhere, including inside other words. That’s what \\b is for.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
The hunt
The str_detect() function slots straight into filter():
# Keep Anne's utterances containing "want" as a whole word.
want <- anne %>%
  filter(str_detect(utterance, "\\bwant\\b"))
  
# Anne's earliest wants (22 months):
want %>%
  filter(age_months == min(age_months)) %>%
  slice(1:15) %>%
  pull(utterance)
 [1] "want juice"           "want juice"           "want juice"           "want these"           "want toys"            "I want the shoes off"
 [7] "want water"           "want foot"            "want"                 "want more"            "want cupboard"        "want babys again"    
[13] "want prams"           "want prams"           "want prams" 
# And her latest wants (33 months):
want %>%
  filter(age_months == max(age_months)) %>%
  slice(1:15) %>%
  pull(utterance)
 [1] "I want black ones"                "want the red"                     "I think want cheese"              "I want my Mummy"

🤔 Think first



Got your three?






Check your thinking





The big ones: a subject has appeared in front of the verb (I want, we don’t want). At 22 months only one utterance out of these fifteen has it; by 33 it’s everywhere. Negation has arrived (don’t want), which barely exists early. And the slot has grown: from single nouns (juice, prams) to phrases (the red, the dirty ones) and even verbs (want do another one). One frame at 22 months; a small grammar around the verb by 33. You may also have caught I think want cheese and which one do you want: the island getting embedded in bigger structures.

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
How does the island develop?
You just found the differences by reading fifteen utterances at each end. But two snapshots can’t show how the change happened: was it gradual, or sudden? For that you need every month in between, and a way to turn one of your observations into a number.
Take the first one: the subject. It’s ideal to count: an utterance either has I before its want or it doesn’t. For each month, we can ask: of Anne’s wants, what share carry the subject?
# Of Anne's wants, per month: what share carry the subject?
iwant_anne <- want %>%
  mutate(with_subject = str_detect(utterance, "\\bI want\\b")) %>%
  group_by(age_months) %>%
  summarise(subject_share = 100 * mean(with_subject),
            n_wants = n())

ggplot(iwant_anne, aes(x = age_months, y = subject_share)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_wants), alpha = .4) +
  labs(title = "Anne's WANT island grows a subject",
       x = "age (months)", y = "% of wants with 'I'",
       size = "wants that month") +
  theme_bw()
Look at the shape and at the dots: they’re sized by how many wants Anne produced that month, because a share computed from twenty utterances deserves less trust than one computed from two hundred. Do you see any convincing patterns in the data?
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
And the other eleven?
One child, one trajectory. But the reading makes a bet about all children. One plot would allow more insight: same pipeline, started from the full table, one panel per child:
# Of each child's wants, per month: what share carry the subject?
iwant_growth <- manchester %>%
  filter(speaker == "CHI") %>%
  mutate(has_want = str_detect(utterance, "\\b(want)\\b")) %>%
  filter(has_want) %>%
  mutate(with_subject = str_detect(utterance, "\\bI (want)\\b")) %>%
  group_by(child, age_months) %>%
  summarise(subject_share = 100 * mean(with_subject),
            n_wants = n(),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(iwant_growth, aes(x = age_months, y = subject_share)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n_wants), alpha = .4) +
  facet_wrap(~child) +
  labs(title = "Twelve islands grow a subject, one child per panel",
       x = "age (months)", y = "% of wants with 'I'",
       size = "wants that month") +
       theme_bw()
Discuss with your neighbour. First describe what you see: are there any clear patterns? Is there one answer for all twelve, or one per panel? Then take Becky: 79% one month, 15% a few months later, back up to 70%. Did her grammar un-develop? If not, what is that sawing, and is it a problem for the theory or for the measurement?

title: 4 · Finding an island
text:
Make the call on “Wanna”
Are these plots a problem for the theory or for the measurement? Let’s inspect our assumptions about measurement. Every count on this page used the pattern \\bwant\\b, but Anne also says wanna. Is wanna + verb part of the same island as want + thing, or a different construction? That’s a theoretical question! Let’s get some more data and read her wanna utterances:
# All of Anne's wanna-utterances.
anne %>%
  filter(str_detect(utterance, "____")) %>%
  pull(utterance)
[1] "I wanna know in that pot"                  "wanna sleeping with Mummy"                 "wanna lie down"                           
  [4] "they wanna go on here"                     "I wanna play"                              "I wanna play"                             
  [7] "I wanna play my sand"                      "I wanna go in the kitchen"                 "wanna come with you and your mummie"      
 [10] "I wanna see"                               "I wanna wanna have tea"                    "wanna sit there"                          
 [13] "wanna play games"                          "wanna play"                                "I wanna see"                              
 [16] "I wanna go in there"                       "don't wanna"                               "don't wanna"                              
 [19] "don't wanna"                               "wanna go in here"                          "me wanna do it"                           
 [22] "wanna put a video on"                      "wanna push it on"                          "wanna go nursery" 
 ...






🤔 Think first



What would Tomasello say?






Check your thinking





He’d note they have different frames: want + thing, wanna + verb, and on his account, different frames are different constructions, possibly not yet connected in Anne’s head. So excluding is defensible. But so is including, if your question is “how often does Anne express wanting?” What you count depends on what you’re asking.





Your turn. Take the twelve-panel chunk above and add wanna to both patterns: the filter() and the with_subject line. Rerun. Does the inclusive ruling change our main results?

title: One Child, Word by Word
text:
The question
How does a child get from single words to grammar?
This week’s reading gives you Tomasello’s answer: not all at once, and not as a system. Each verb starts out as its own island, its own little construction, with its own frame learned from use (want + thing; more + thing). Grammar, on this account, is what emerges as the islands grow and connect. It’s a radical claim, because the traditional picture (i.e., Chomsky’s) says grammatical knowledge is general from the start, not built verb by verb.
Radical claims need evidence, and this one makes a checkable prediction: a two-year-old’s verbs should be uneven: some flexible, some frozen, each on its own schedule. Today you check it, on the corpus that was collected to check it: you’ll follow Anne from her second birthday toward her third, watch one island grow, and then ask whether what you found holds across eleven more children.

title: 1 · Meet the data
text:
Twelve children learning to talk
Between 1998 and 2001, researchers in Manchester recorded twelve English children at home, playing and talking with their mothers: an hour at a time, twice in every three-week period, from around each child’s second birthday until around their third. The children are known by first names: Anne, Aran, Becky, Carl, Dominic, Gail, Joel, John, Liz, Nicole, Ruth and Warren.
This is the Manchester corpus (Theakston, Lieven, Pine & Rowland, 2001). It was collected to test the theory you read this week: that children build grammar verb by verb, and it is publicly available through CHILDES, the international database of child language.
Everything the children and mothers said was transcribed. We have converted those transcripts into one table, where each row is one utterance: one thing one person said at one moment.







column
what it contains




child
which child’s recording this is ("Anne", "Becky", …)


age_months
the child’s age at that recording, in months


speaker
who is talking: "CHI" (the child) or "MOT" (the mother)


utterance
what they said


num_tokens
how many words that is



So the row Anne · 26 · CHI · "want some juice" · 3 means: Anne, aged 2;2, said want some juice: three words.

The mothers talk a lot in these recordings. Which column would you use to keep only the children’s utterances?

speaker: filtering for speaker == "CHI" keeps the child’s own speech. child tells you whose recording it is; even in Anne’s files, half the rows are her mother.

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text:
The measure
Mean Length of Utterance (MLU): the average number of words per utterance. It sounds almost too simple, and yet since Brown (1973) it has been the standard yardstick of early grammar, for a good reason: to say longer things, you have to combine more things. A child at MLU 1.5 is mostly naming; a child at MLU 3.5 is building sentences. You already have everything you need: num_tokens holds each utterance’s length, and age_months groups utterances into months of recording.

title: Mean Length of Utterance

Task 2: Plot it
Before plotting, one prediction. Bring back Anne’s utterances from her oldest age (you built this on the last page):

anne %>%
  filter(age_months == max(age_months)) %>%

Just under 3. If you guessed higher, look again at how many one- and two-word turns sit between the long ones: yeah, no, there. The mean drags every short reply along with the impressively long sentences. The plot shows how she gets there from ~1.5: how fast, and how smoothly.

title: Mean Length of Utterance
text:
Task 3: Read the plot
With your partner:
1 · The verdict on your sentence. On the last page you wrote one sentence about what changed between Anne’s first and last recordings. Does the curve agree with you? And is there anything you noticed by looking at her data that a per-month average could never show?
2 · Find a dip. Somewhere the curve drops from one month to the next. Is Anne’s language deteriorating here?






🤔 Think first



Before you answer. Look at n_utts across the months. Some months have roughly double the utterances of others. Why?






Check your thinking





Anne was recorded about twice every three weeks, but our ages are rounded to the month, so some months contain two recording sessions bundled together, and some just one. A mean over 1,000 utterances is steadier than a mean over 500; and a single session catches a single day’s mood, sleep, and lunch. We’ll see later on how we can represent this in a plot.





In Task 1, you computed MLU per month for Anne. The same pipeline computes it for all twelve children at once: the only change is where you start, and what you group by:
# MLU per month, for every child: start from the FULL table this time.
mlu_all <- ____ %>%                       # not anne - which table has everyone?
  filter(speaker == "CHI") %>%
  group_by(child, ____) %>%               # group by child AND month
  summarise(mlu = mean(num_tokens),
            .groups = "drop")

mlu_all
Grouping by two columns gives one row per child per month. Twelve growth curves in one table. (.groups = "drop" just tells R to hand back a plain table afterwards; without it you get a harmless warning.)

  labs(title = "Anne among the twelve",
       x = "age (months)", y = "MLU (words)") +
  theme_bw()

Interpret the plot
With your partner, discuss the following: How much do twelve normally-developing children differ at the same age? Find the widest vertical spread. How many months of development does that gap correspond to along the curve?






One honest limit



MLU says Anne’s and the other children’s utterances got longer, but it says nothing about what’s in them. Want some juice and Mummy sock fall both score three words, but they are very different achievements. Same number, different grammar. Next block, we look inside the utterances themselves.

title: 6 · Open questions
text: If you’re interested, every question below can be tackled with the tools you used today; and not everything below has a known answer!

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
1 · The second island
Everything today was WANT. Pick another verb (e.g., have, like, get, put) and give it the full treatment: read early and late hits, then plot its subject-share across the twelve children.
The question that makes this interesting: within one child, do the two islands grow their subject at the same time? If grammar is one system, they should move together. If each island grows from its own use, WANT might have a subject months before LIKE does. Nobody knows the answer, yet!
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
2 · The Warren problem
Have a look at Warren’s panel of word islands. It starts near 70%, meaning that he uses the subject already at 22 months, before Anne’s has begun. Is this precocious grammar, or one frozen chunk? Try to read his early I wants. If the slot varies (I want juice, I want teddy, I want down), the frame is productive. If it’s the same phrase on repeat, it’s a formula wearing a subject. Figure out what’s going on with Warren by looking at the data.
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
3 · The error nobody taught
Children say things no adult ever said to them: goed, comed, falled, foots, mouses. These are the classic evidence that children build rules rather than copy. You can’t imitate what nobody says.
Try to detect them: "\\b(goed|comed|falled|breaked|foots|mouses|sheeps)\\b" and extend the net with your own guesses. Which children produce them, and at what ages? And then check the mothers. If an error truly has a frequency of zero in the input, what does its existence tell you, and can either theory claim it?
crumbs: Workshop 1 · One Child, Word by Word

title: 6 · Open questions
text:
4 · What’s that → what’s what?
Questions have their own development: what and where come early; why, famously, arrives late and then detonates. Track the four question words: what, where, who, why per 100 utterances across age, for a child of your choice. When does why explode? And is the explosion a language fact or a cognition fact. What does a child need to understand before why is worth asking?

Task 1: The two curves
Pair 1 went from sixteen words to three on tangram B. But that’s one pair, one shape. Maybe they were unusual. To find out if it’s the general pattern, average across all 83 pairs and all twelve shapes: for each repetition, how long is the director’s average message?

# Question 1 — for each repetition, the director's average message length.
reduction <- tangrams %>%
  filter(role == "____") %>%      # whose messages? the ones doing the describing
  group_by(____) %>%              # what do we want the progression across?
  summarise(mean_words = mean(____)) 

reduction
And there’s a second question hiding underneath. Saying less could mean the matchers understood less. So let’s measure that too: for each repetition, how often did the matcher pick the right shape? Two questions, two near-identical pipelines:
# Question 2 — for each repetition, how often the matcher was right.
accuracy <- tangrams %>%
  group_by(repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_correct = 100 * mean(____))   # which column is 1-for-right, 0-for-wrong?

title: Less and less, better and better
text:
Task 3: Watch the hedging disappear
On the last page you noticed the tentative words (i.e., kinda looks like, maybe) dropping out. Those are hedges: the words we add when we’re unsure and offering a guess, rather than stating something we both know. If common ground really is what makes them unnecessary, hedges should fade round by round. Let’s count them.
To find a hedge, we check whether a message contains any of a short list of hedge words. str_detect with the | (“or”) pattern does it (that is, “looks like|kinda|maybe|sort of”). This net would catch looks like, kinda, maybe, or sort of:
Hedges (looks like, kinda, maybe, sort of) are the grammar of not-yet-knowing-together. Count their disappearance:
tangrams %>%
  filter(role == "director") %>%
  mutate(hedged = str_detect(message, ____)) %>%
  group_by(repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_hedged = 100 * mean(hedged, na.rm = TRUE))
# A tibble: 6 × 2
  repetition pct_hedged
       <dbl>      <dbl>
1          1         29
2          2          9
3          3          3
4          4          1
5          5          1
6          6          0
Nearly a third of round-one messages hedge; by round six, none do. The tentativeness of not-yet-knowing-together evaporates. Try to widen the net (I think, possibly, seems) and check the story survives your ruling. Maybe it’s easier to see this as plot:
# Pipe the hedge table straight into a plot.
tangrams %>%
  filter(role == "director") %>%
  mutate(hedged = str_detect(message, "looks like|kinda|maybe|sort of")) %>%
  group_by(repetition) %>%
  summarise(pct_hedged = 100 * mean(hedged, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = ____, y = ____)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "____",
       x = "repetition", y = "% of messages that hedge") +
  theme_bw()

So far: when two people refer to the same things again and again, their descriptions get shorter, their hedges disappear, their accuracy climbs, and each pair ends up with private names that only work between them. Next: what happens when you’re describing not to one partner, but to a whole group at once?

title: 1 · Meet the data
text:
Communities inventing words
In this dataset, we have communities of four or eight people, inventing words for shapes that had no names (Raviv, Meyer & Lev-Ari, 2019). One quick reminder of a single turn, because its pieces become the columns of our table. One person (the producer) saw a shape and typed a made-up word for it. Their partner picked the shape they thought it meant: a hit if they were right, a miss if they were wrong. Then they swapped roles and moved on, pair after pair, for fourteen rounds.
At the start, everyone typed different nonsense. Round by round, each community drifted toward words it came to share: a small language, different in every group. Every one of those turns is in the dataset below, one row each: one word that one person produced for one shape.
The clever part is the design: some communities were large and some were small. That’s the comparison we’ll come back to. For now, just meet the data. We’ve put every turn into one table, where each row is one word that one person produced for one shape:







column

community
the size of the group: "big" or "small"


group
which group it was ("g01" … "g24")


round
which round of the game (1-14) — the game’s clock


item
which shape was being described (a number, 1-28)


shape
the shape’s family (a rough visual category)


producer
which person in the group typed the word


word
the made-up word they typed


correct
did the partner pick the right shape? (1 = yes, 0 = no)

Task 1: Does communication get better?
You watched a couple of groups drift from chaos toward a shared word. If that’s really happening across the board, then communication should succeed more often in later rounds: partners picking the right shape more and more as the shared words settle in.
The correct column is 1 for a hit, 0 for a miss. The average of a column of 1s and 0s is just the proportion of 1s, so mean(correct) per round is the success rate that round.

section: Task 2: Small communities versus large ones
text:
Task 2: Small communities versus large ones
Now the real question. Before you run anything, commit to a guess.

By the final round, which communities communicate better: the small ones (four people) or the large ones (eight)?

Lock it in. Now build the plot below, and watch how far apart the two lines end up.


To compare the two, we group by round and community, then give each community its own coloured line:
by_community <- lang %>%
  group_by(round, ___) %>%          # round AND ??
  summarise(pct_correct = 100 * mean(correct, na.rm = T), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(by_community, aes(x = round, y = pct_correct,
                         colour = ___)) +        # colour by community
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(title = "Bigger communities build better languages",
       x = "round", y = "% of guesses correct",
       colour = "community") +
  theme_bw()
Both lines climb: every community’s language improves. But after the first few rounds, the large-community line pulls clear and stays ahead, finishing near 70% while the small communities level off around 55%. If you bet on the small ones you’re in good company: most people do, and the data says the opposite. More people, better communication. But why?

title: Exercise 1 · Does communication improve?
section: Task 3: Why would a bigger community be better?
text:
Task 3: Why would a bigger community be better?
This is the genuinely surprising result: you’d expect a big, sprawling group to struggle. Talk it through with your partner: why might a bigger community end up communicating better?
Here’s the shape of the answer, to hold in mind. In a small group, you talk to the same two or three people every round, so you can get away with quirky, private words (like the pair last week who called one of the tangrams “praying monk”). It works, but only because you all know each other’s quirks. In a big group you keep meeting different partners, so a private quirk falls flat with the next person. Only words that work for everybody survive.
But how does a word come to “work for everybody”? Let’s go find the answer in the data.

title: Open questions
text:
1 · The spread behind the averages
Those two tidy lines from Exercise 1 are averages, and each one hides twelve separate communities. Let’s meet the crowd behind the average: draw every community as its own faint line, coloured by size. An answer would involve group = group inside aes(): it tells ggplot to draw one line per group. Now the real question: do the big communities all beat the small ones, or do they just tend to? Watch how far the two clouds overlap.

title: Open questions
text:
2 · Which shapes fought back?
Some shapes are easy to name; others resist to the very end. For one community, work out each shape’s success rate in the final round and find the stubborn ones. Then read the words that community used for its hardest shape. Did they ever settle on a shared root for it, the way they did on fem-? A shape with no agreed word is a small window into why some meanings are harder to share than others.

title: Open questions
section: 3 · Does a fast start mean a strong finish?
text:
3 · Does a fast start mean a strong finish?
Some communities find their feet quickly, others take a while. For each community, find the first round it crossed 50% accuracy, then compare that with where it finished. Do the quick starters also finish highest, or can a slow starter overtake late? There’s no guarantee that the community which communicates soonest is the one that communicates best by the end. The data will tell you which it is.

title: Open questions
text:
4 · Invent your own measure
You’ve measured two things about a language being born: whether it works (accuracy) and how its words are shaped (length). Now invent a third: something you’re curious about, turned into a number you can compute for each round. A few to spark ideas:

Vocabulary size: how many different words is a community juggling for one shape each round? Does it balloon early, then shrink as they prune?
Agreement: what share of a community uses the single most common word for a shape?

text:
5 · Make something cool
Every plot so far has been a line chart. Break the mould. Make one visualisation that shows something about these languages being born that a line chart can’t, and make it beautiful. Some thoughts:
